segments.text: This final chapter draws together the resource, exploration, and engineering concepts of earlier chapters into the broader practice of applying geological knowledge for direct economic and societal benefit — the culminating, most explicitly “applied” chapter of the subject.
Determining whether a geological material is genuinely worth extracting requires evaluating it against several combined factors: the deposit’s
(concentration of the valuable material) and total

(quantity available), the costs of extraction and processing (strongly influenced by depth, location, accessibility, and the specific extraction method required), and prevailing and reasonably projected future market prices for the material — since all of these factors can and do change over time (particularly market price, which is often genuinely volatile), a specific deposit’s economic viability is not a fixed, permanent geological fact but a conclusion that must be periodically reassessed as conditions change.
Building on the general exploration workflow of Chapter 10,

is the specific practical technique of collecting representative physical material (from surface outcrops, trenches, or drill core) for laboratory analysis to determine actual mineral grade and content. Because ore deposits are frequently significantly heterogeneous (grade can vary considerably even over comparatively short distances within a single deposit), a careful, systematic, and appropriately dense sampling strategy is essential to obtain a genuinely representative and reliable estimate of a deposit’s overall average grade, rather than one distorted by chance sampling of unusually rich or unusually poor localised zones.

applies geological understanding directly and continuously throughout the active, ongoing process of mineral extraction — including precisely and continuously delineating the exact boundaries and internal grade distribution of the ore body as mining proceeds and further data becomes available, and providing continuously updated geological input and guidance to ongoing mine planning and design decisions (influencing, for example, the choice between open-pit and underground mining methods, chosen based specifically on the ore body’s depth, shape, and surrounding rock stability characteristics).

blocks.text: 3. Groundwater and other applied geological investigations

segments.text: Beyond the general engineering-geology treatment of groundwater in Chapter 9, applied geological investigation specifically for water-resource development requires appropriately identifying and characterising productive aquifers (permeable rock or sediment layers capable of yielding useful water quantities), estimating their sustainable yield, and properly assessing water quality — since over-extraction beyond an aquifer’s natural sustainable recharge rate can cause serious long-term problems, including significant water-table decline, land subsidence, and, in coastal areas specifically, saltwater intrusion into what was previously a freshwater aquifer.

blocks.text: 4. Remote sensing and geological mapping applications

segments.text: (using satellite or aerial imagery, across various parts of the electromagnetic spectrum, connecting to Physics Chapter III) helps geologists efficiently recognize broad-scale geological patterns — including major rock unit boundaries, structural lineaments (surface expressions of underlying faults or major joint sets), and characteristic alteration zones associated with certain types of mineralisation — over large areas rapidly and comparatively inexpensively, substantially guiding and focusing where more detailed, and inherently more expensive, ground-based mapping and exploration effort should subsequently be concentrated.

At syllabus level, understanding how the concepts of this entire Paper — ore genesis, exploration workflow, economic evaluation, and applied investigation — combine and apply concretely to specific, real, named Pakistani deposits and occurrences is the practical, integrative capstone of the subject; where an older syllabus reference uses a locality spelling that differs from the modern accepted name, the modern spelling should generally be used in written answers, while still recognising and correctly cross-referencing the original syllabus term.

items.text: Economic viability of a geological material depends jointly on grade, tonnage, extraction/processing cost, and market price — none of which are permanently fixed, so viability must be periodically reassessed as conditions change.
Because ore grade is frequently heterogeneous even within a single deposit, systematic and adequately dense sampling is essential for a reliable overall grade estimate.
Mining geology continuously updates ore-body delineation and directly informs ongoing mine planning and method-selection decisions throughout active extraction.
Sustainable aquifer management requires balancing extraction against natural recharge rate, since over-extraction can cause water-table decline, subsidence, or (in coastal areas) saltwater intrusion.
Remote sensing efficiently identifies broad-scale geological patterns over large areas, effectively guiding where more detailed and costly ground-based exploration should subsequently focus.
